title: Root Canal Retreatment vs Extraction: Weighing the Options
metaTitle: Root Canal Retreatment vs Extraction: How to Decide
metaDescription: If a root canal failed, should you redo it or pull the tooth? Compare retreatment and extraction, replacement options, and how a Markham dentist helps decide.
secondaryKeywords: redo root canal or pull tooth
excerpt: If a root canal failed, you can often choose between retreatment to save the tooth or extraction with a replacement. Here is how to weigh the options.
heroImageAlt: Split illustration showing a tooth undergoing retreatment on one side and an extraction site with an implant on the other.
bodyHtml:
If a root canal has failed, you generally have two main paths: retreatment to try to save the natural tooth, or extraction followed by a replacement such as an implant or bridge. Neither is automatically the right answer. The best choice depends on how much healthy tooth remains, why the first treatment did not hold, your overall oral health, and your own priorities around time, cost, and keeping a natural tooth. A dentist assesses the tooth and helps you weigh the options.

Why keeping a natural tooth often comes first

Dentistry generally leans toward preserving your own tooth when that is realistic. A natural tooth maintains the surrounding bone, keeps neighbouring teeth stable, and preserves your natural bite in ways replacements aim to imitate but cannot perfectly match. That is why retreatment is frequently considered before extraction — not as a guarantee, but as a reasonable first option when the tooth has a good chance of healing.

What retreatment involves

In retreatment, the dentist reopens the tooth, removes the previous root canal filling material, cleans and disinfects the canals again, looks for anything missed the first time (such as an extra canal), and re-seals the tooth. The tooth then needs a new permanent restoration. You can learn more about root canal retreatment at Smile Dental Arts Centre and what the process typically includes.

Retreatment tends to be considered when enough sound tooth structure remains, the tooth is restorable, and the gum and bone support are reasonable. It keeps your natural tooth and avoids the need for a replacement, though like any treatment it does not succeed in every case.

When extraction may be the better route

Sometimes a tooth is too damaged to save well. Extraction may be the more sensible option when:

  • The tooth is cracked deep below the gum or badly broken down.
  • There is severe bone loss or advanced gum disease around it.
  • Retreatment has already been tried and the problem persists.
  • The long-term outlook for saving the tooth is poor.

If a tooth is removed, it is usually wise to plan how to replace it, because a gap can let neighbouring teeth drift and can affect chewing and bone over time. Replacement options include a dental implant, a fixed bridge, or a removable partial denture, each with its own trade-offs to discuss with your dentist.

Weighing the options together

There is no universal winner between retreatment and extraction. The best decision balances the clinical picture with what matters to you, and it is worth taking the time to understand both routes before committing. A few things worth comparing with your dentist:

  • Keeping your natural tooth — retreatment preserves it; extraction does not.
  • Overall treatment journey — extraction plus a replacement such as an implant can involve several stages and healing time.
  • Cost over time — the cheaper option up front is not always the cheaper option in the long run; costs vary and should be discussed directly.
  • The tooth's prospects — a tooth with a good chance of healing is a strong candidate for retreatment; one with a poor outlook may not be.

Is it always better to save the tooth?

Not always. Saving a tooth is often preferable, but when a tooth's outlook is poor, a well-planned extraction and replacement can be the healthier long-term choice. The assessment matters more than any blanket rule.

Does an extracted tooth have to be replaced?

Replacing it is usually recommended to protect your bite and neighbouring teeth, but the right option depends on the location and your circumstances.

How many times can a root canal be retreated?

Retreatment can sometimes be done more than once, but each attempt removes a little more tooth structure, so the realistic options narrow over time. Your dentist will advise whether further retreatment is sensible for your tooth.

Making the decision with guidance

Because so much depends on the individual tooth, this is a decision to make with a dentist who can examine it and review the X-rays. Dr. Neda Kadivar is a general and family dentist with over 20 years of experience who can discuss retreatment and replacement considerations at the dental team at Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham, Ontario.

This article is general information and not a substitute for professional dental advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with a licensed dentist about your specific situation.
